fixes.explanation: Right. After Elijah lays out the plan, the people answered, “What you say is good.” (1 Kings 18:24) Remember, they'd said nothing a moment before. Now they're on board.

The text says otherwise, friend. When Elijah lays out the plan, the people answer, “What you say is good.” (1 Kings 18:24) They'd been silent a few verses earlier, so this is a change. Now they agree to the test.

Yes, friend. Elijah says to the prophets of Baal, "Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first." (1 Kings 18:25) They have four hundred and fifty prophets to his one, so they go first. Then he adds, "…do not light the fire."

Silence. The text says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) They shouted from morning until noon. All that effort, and no one answered.

Not a spark, friend. The text says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) Elijah had told them not to light the fire (1 Kings 18:25). A spark from above would have been an answer, and the text says no one answered.

Thunder isn't what the text reports, friend. It says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) They shouted from morning until noon. What they got was no sound and no answer.

It's true, friend, and Elijah is on a ROLL. He says, "Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!" (1 Kings 18:27) That's a whole list of excuses, the kind you'd text when you're ducking a group dinner. Journey and sleeping are both right there. He's taunting the prophets of Baal the whole way through.

The text doesn't mention Ahab, king of Israel, here, friend. It says they "…kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice." (1 Kings 18:29) The marker the text gives is the time of day. And the verse ends, "…no one answered, no one paid attention."

He sure does. The text says he "…repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down." (1 Kings 18:30) The altar was torn down, and Elijah is the one who repaired it. He does it right after telling the people, “Come near to me.”

Elijah doesn't leave it that way. The text says, "…he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down." (1 Kings 18:30) It had been torn down, and he repaired it. That's the altar of the LORD getting put back together.

That's the reason the text gives. Elijah took twelve stones, "one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob…" (1 Kings 18:31) These are the tribes the word of the LORD came to, saying Israel would be their name. Twelve tribes, twelve stones.

The text doesn't count any helpers here. It says he took twelve stones, "one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob…" (1 Kings 18:31) So the number is about the tribes, not the helpers. Twelve stones, twelve tribes.

Water, friend. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." (1 Kings 18:34) That's water on a bull and wood that are already on the altar. I've never seen a baker do that, and I've seen plenty.

It's true, friend, and the text counts every round. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." Then he says, “Do it a second time,” and then, “Do it a third time,” (1 Kings 18:34) and they did each one. That's three rounds of four waterpots. My mustache got tired just counting.

There's nothing about the drought in this prayer, friend. Elijah asks, "…let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command." (1 Kings 18:36) The prayer is about who God is and whom Elijah serves. Rain isn't what he asks for here.

It's true, friend, and it's right there in the prayer. Elijah says, "Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again." (1 Kings 18:37) He asks twice, plain and bold. And he says why: so the people will know.

Nothing in the text says they ran, friend, or that they were afraid. It says, "When all the people saw this, they fell facedown…" (1 Kings 18:39) Then they say, “The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!” Down on their faces, and speaking.

That's it. Elijah says to Ahab, king of Israel, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain." (1 Kings 18:41) He says it before the servant reports any cloud. Elijah is already talking about the sound of rain.

No army marching in this scene. Elijah tells Ahab, king of Israel, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain." (1 Kings 18:41) What he hears is rain, not soldiers. And Ahab does go up to eat and drink.

A cloud. On the seventh time the servant reports, "There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea." (1 Kings 18:44) That's a cloud about the size of a hand. Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” before he got that report.

Not a bird, friend. The servant reports, "There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea." (1 Kings 18:44) It's a cloud, and a small one, rising. Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” and the report came on the seventh.

No second sacrifice in this message, friend. Elijah says, “Go and tell Ahab, ‘Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’” (1 Kings 18:44) Ahab is the king of Israel. That's a message about a chariot and the rain, not another round at the altar.

Not Bethel, friend. The text says, "So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:45) The sky is dark with clouds and wind, heavy rain is falling, and Ahab, Israel's king, takes off. Bethel never even makes it into the verse.
